extracted.intended_audience: American patrons of art, artists, and literate readers interested in 19th‑century art criticism and Roman affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for assessing artists' work, commissioning sculpture and paintings, and appropriate patron behavior as discussed in a 19th‑century letter from Rome. Covers compositional qualities, originality, artist remuneration, and fair selection procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of design and heartfelt message
rubrics_metrics.description: The design of a picture should be original and not merely an imitation; it should be 'laden with any message from the heart.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticizes works whose design is 'never original' and which lack a message from the heart; implies preference for works that convey genuine feeling and original conception (contrast given between Terry and Hicks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist as original observer and thinker
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist should be 'a man of ideas, an original observer, and with a poetic heart.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holds up Hicks as example: originality, thoughtful study, and poetic sensibility are central qualities that distinguish promising artists from mere imitators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coloring derived from thoughtful study (not mere imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of coloring ought to be derived from thoughtful study rather than mere imitation of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author's praise for Hicks notes that his coloring shows the fineness of his organization and results from study; color systems should be principled and studied, not slavish copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and grouping for large multi-figure works
rubrics_metrics.description: Large pictures should have original, noble designs with highly effective grouping of figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Hicks's design for a large picture of many figures is praised for original design and effective grouping; successful large compositions require adequate resources (models, time) to realize the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landscape painting should capture the spirit, not just copy scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Landscape painters should aim for a 'transfusion of the spirit' of scenes rather than mere copies upon canvas of magnificent views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that American landscape painting should not simply reproduce scenery but convey the divinity/spirit of nature; recommends studying how to achieve harmony of varied elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of foreign study for compositional instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: A few years' study in places like Italy is valuable because ruins and the union of nature and man provide instruction in composition and harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studying where 'Nature herself has worked with man' helps artists learn how to accomplish unity and harmony in compositions and equips them to adapt to other climates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositional balance and legibility at a distance
rubrics_metrics.description: A fine work of art must have a beautiful overall effect at a distance where details are not discernible; balance of forms and harmony are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Goethe: a work should read well at the first glance; Crawford's group praised for graceful, simple, harmonious composition and the freedom with which light and air play in and out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory should serve action and composition, not be insipid
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegorical figures are acceptable when they give poetic sense and natural support for action, not when they result in insipid or merely decorative allegory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defends the winged figure in Crawford's group as providing poetic sense and a natural occasion for the horse and rider's action; warns against empty allegory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical and motion study for equestrian statues
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of an equestrian statue demands serious study of the anatomy and action of the horse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that the study of horse anatomy and action is 'naturally most desirable' and a rich subject for artists, implying that those who undertake equestrian statues must be prepared by specific study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection by impartial committee for public commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public commissions (e.g., equestrian statues) should be awarded by a committee of impartial judges who look only to merit and are free of personal interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommends setting aside 'mean squabbles and jealousies' and allowing each artist to offer a design so the best may be chosen; questions belief that such an impartial committee is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open submission and preference for the best design
rubrics_metrics.description: Each artist should be permitted to submit designs and the best design should receive the commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States explicitly: 'let each artist offer his design for an equestrian statue of Washington, and let the best have the preference.' Supports open competition rather than favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair payment including remuneration for design and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Patrons must pay the artist fairly for time spent designing and modelling as well as for execution; paying only for materials or final product cheats the artist of their thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorandum and commentary stress that artists need funds for studio rent, assistants, models, and materials; paying too little (or only for labor but not thought) is unjust and common among American patrons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patrons should not change commissions after modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Patrons must avoid changing their minds after a statue (or work) has been modelled; such behavior is injurious and unjust to the artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that American patrons have been known to change their minds when the statue is modelled, causing offense and harm; implies contractual and moral obligation to respect commissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the real costs of artistic study abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: The common belief that a student of art can live in Italy on $300–$400 a year is false; adequate funds (suggested $1,000/year) are needed to pursue studies properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides specific cost estimates: rent, journeyman wages, model pay, marble pricing, and life‑size statue fees ($1,000–$5,000) to correct patrons' misperceptions about the expense of true artistic study and production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patron conduct: generosity tempered by education in the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Patrons should be educated about the processes and costs of art so their generosity does not become inadvertent cruelty (e.g., forcing artists to suffer unnecessarily or bargaining down prices unfairly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against romanticizing artists' suffering; admonishes 'American Mæcenas' for bargaining habits and lack of knowledge that lead to underpaying or imposing hardship on artists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge artists by medium‑specific mastery and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess an artist's work in the context of their medium and training—excellence in busts does not automatically translate to excellence in ideal statues or other genres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Powers is praised for busts (clear conception and execution) but criticized in larger ideal treatments due to limited study of the human body; consider medium‑specific discipline when evaluating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public display and multiple good works benefit artistic growth
rubrics_metrics.description: The more quality works made publicly available in daylight, the more artists 'germinate'—public exposure and variety stimulate artistic development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates that abundant good works for the people to see freely will encourage artistic production and raise standards; implies patronage should support public visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic recognition principle (political conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: A republican government should, in principle, be recognized by other republican nations when it is the government chosen by the people and can sustain itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues the only dignified ground for a republic is to recognize governments chosen by their people; uses Mr. Cass's non‑recognition of Rome's government as an example of offending the Romans and missing a principled opportunity.
